etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English intelligence, from Old French intelligence, from Latin intelligentia, which is from inter- (“between”) + legere (“choose, pick out, read”), or Proto-Italic *legō (“to care”). Doublet of intelligentsia.

definitions.definition: (chiefly uncountable) Capacity of mind, especially to understand principles, truths, facts or meanings, acquire knowledge, and apply it to practice; the ability to comprehend and learn; the ability to process sentient experience to generate true beliefs with a justified degree of confidence.

quote.citation: 1912 October, Edgar Rice Burroughs, “Tarzan of the Apes”, in The All-Story, New York, N.Y.: Frank A. Munsey Co., →OCLC; republished as chapter 5, in Tarzan of the Apes, New York, N.Y.: A. L. Burt Company, 1914 June, →OCLC:
quote.text: Not so, however, with Tarzan, the man-child. His life amidst the dangers of the jungle had taught him to meet emergencies with self-confidence, and his higher intelligence resulted in a quickness of mental action far beyond the powers of the apes.

quote.citation: 1936 Feb., F. Scott Fitzgerald, "The Crack-Up", Esquire:
quote.text: ...the test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in the mind at the same time, and still retain the ability to function.

quote.citation: 2013 July 19, Ian Sample, “Irregular bedtimes may affect children's brains”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 6, page 34:
quote.text: Irregular bedtimes may disrupt healthy brain development in young children, according to a study of intelligence and sleeping habits.  ¶ Going to bed at a different time each night affected girls more than boys, but both fared worse on mental tasks than children who had a set bedtime, researchers found.

definitions.definition: (chiefly uncountable) The quality of making use or having made use of such capacities: depth of understanding, mental quickness.

quote.citation: 2018, Dalai Lama, translated by Dhondup Tsering, Introduction to Buddhism, →ISBN, page 8:
quote.text: From a religious point of view, a bodhisattva with sharp faculties and great intelligence can cause a tremendous upheaval if he or she misuses that power under the influence of negative emotions, like attachment and hatred.

definitions.definition: (countable) An entity that has such capacities.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto LXXXV:
quote.text: The great Intelligences fair / That range above our mortal state, / In circle round the blessed gate, / Received and gave him welcome there.

quote.citation: 1898, H.G. Wells, The War of the Worlds, London: William Heinemann, page 102:
quote.text: The living intelligence, the Martian within the hood, was slain and splashed to the four winds of heaven, and the thing was now but a mere intricate device of metal whirling to destruction.

quote.citation: 1936, Rollo Ahmed, The Black Art, London: Long, page 275:
quote.text: But there are latent powers within man alone that are not yet fully understood and [...] we cannot definitely state what is, and what is not, due to the interference or influence of discarnate intelligences.

quote.citation: 1981, William Irwin Thompson, The Time Falling Bodies Take to Light: Mythology, Sexuality and the Origins of Culture, London: Rider/Hutchinson & Co., page 228:
quote.text: He passes beyond the projections and thought forms of his own creation to the wholly other and independent world of the angelic intelligences.

definitions.definition: (chiefly uncountable) Information, often secret, about an enemy or about hostile activities.

quote.citation: 2019 February 27, Drachinifel, 40:01 from the start, in The Battle of Samar - Odds? What are those?‎[1], archived from the original on 3 November 2022:
quote.text: Their lack of good intelligence also meant that they vastly overestimated the size of their foes for far too long, hails of armor-piercing shells doing comparatively little damage compared to the high explosive that they should have been using.

definitions.definition: (countable) A political or military department, agency or unit designed to gather information, usually secret, about the enemy or about hostile activities.

quote.citation: 1702–1704, Edward [Hyde, 1st] Earl of Clarendon, “(please specify |book=I to XVI)”, in The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England, Begun in the Year 1641. […], Oxford, Oxfordshire: Printed at the Theater, published 1707, →OCLC:
quote.text: He lived rather in a fair intelligence than any friendship with the favourite
